findings.title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

findings.title: Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused
findings.body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure
findings.body: Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

findings.title: Failed work items are still marked offset-complete
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

findings.title: Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

findings.title: Error-handling test is timing-dependent and asserts the wrong outcome
findings.body: The test makes the first result processor call raise and the second succeed, then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in its finally block even when processing raised, so both offsets become complete and the background commit loop should eventually commit the partition. The test only sleeps 0.2 seconds after processing finishes, while the commit loop wakes every 1 second, so it usually passes before the commit happens and will flake when setup or processing takes slightly longer. It therefore does not reliably verify the intended error semantics; it should either assert the actual expected commit behavior or the production code should keep failed offsets outstanding.
